messages.content:
Assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category. Here are worked examples, then the case to code.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: I21

Example 3
Hospital course: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever, rigors, dysuria and right flank tenderness. Urine microscopy showed pyuria and culture grew Escherichia coli. Computed tomography showed a swollen right kidney with no abscess. She improved on intravenous ceftriaxone.
Answer: N10

Example 4
Hospital course: An 81-year-old woman was brought in after a fall at home. She could not weight-bear and the right leg was shortened and externally rotated. A pelvic radiograph showed a displaced subcapital fracture of the right femoral neck. She underwent hemiarthroplasty on day one.
Answer: S72

Example 5
Hospital course: A 19-year-old man presented with 18 hours of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and a low-grade fever. There was guarding at McBurney's point and the white cell count was 15.2. Laparoscopy confirmed an inflamed, non-perforated appendix.
Answer: K35

Example 6
Hospital course: A 64-year-old woman with a history of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma treated five years earlier presented with progressive thoracic back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging showed deposits in T7 and T9 with no cord compression. Biopsy confirmed deposits of breast origin and she received palliative radiotherapy to the spine.
Answer: C79

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 46-year-old male

Admission date: [DATE]

Discharge date: [DATE]

Medical history: None reported except exertional dyspnea.

Chief complaint: Exertional dyspnea

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a chief complaint of exertional dyspnea. Physical examination revealed a systolic mitral murmur and a diastolic aortic murmur. TTE revealed a noncoronary SVA protruding into the mitral anterior leaflet, leading to moderate mitral regurgitation, severe aortic insufficiency, and a dilated aortic root. The ascending aorta measured 54-mm, and the left ventricular diastolic diameter was 75-mm, with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 66%. No ventricular septal defect was detected. Coronary CTA showed no abnormalities or stenoses found in the coronary tree and the sac of the noncoronary SVA (measuring 36 × 47 × 51 mm) was protruding into the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve. Surgery was performed via median sternotomy. The thickening of the wall of the tricuspid aortic valve and ascending aortic wall was consistent with inflammation. The patient underwent mitral valve and aortic valve replacement and replacement of the ascending aorta with an artificial vessel. Antibiotics were administered for 5 weeks. Follow-up TTE showed satisfactory functioning of both replaced valves. Aortic CTA demonstrated restoration of the normal anatomical relationship at the aortic root. The patient was discharged in stable condition.
Discharge diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge instructions: The patient was advised to follow-up with a primary care physician and cardiologist and adhere to medication and lifestyle modification recommendations.

Answer with the three-character category only.

text:
The case describes a sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (SVA) of the noncoronary sinus, which is a congenital malformation of the aortic sinus. ICD-10 codes it at Q25.4 (other congenital malformations of the aorta) or Q25.3 or Q24.8. The alternative is acquired aortic aneurysm, I71. The picture also includes severe aortic insufficiency and mitral regurgitation, and the wall inflammation with 5 weeks of antibiotics suggests infection, possibly endocarditis.

The aneurysm itself is the main problem. Its sac protrudes into the mitral anterior leaflet, and the surgery addressed the aneurysm along with the valves and ascending aorta. The patient had no prior history, and the SVA is most likely congenital, so Q25 fits. The chief complaint of exertional dyspnea was caused by valvular disease secondary to the SVA, but the underlying condition is the SVA.

An alternative would be I35 (nonrheumatic aortic valve disorders), since the aortic insufficiency was severe. The five weeks of antibiotics point to infective endocarditis (I33), but the summary does not state this explicitly. It says only that the wall thickening was "consistent with inflammation". The diagnosis section is withheld, so the diagnosis is most likely SVA, and I chose Q25.

**Q25**
